text:
sam: Heads up — after the kubelet upgrade our canary shows a 15% p99 regression on short-chat workloads. I ran an nsys capture but the GPU kernel lanes are almost empty, only driver prep + memcpy. suspect traces are incomplete due to container sandboxing
priya: ugh. did you run nsys inside the pod or exec into the container? permission issues often strip NV libs events
sam: exec into the pod and ran `nsys profile --output=/tmp/capture` inside the container. nsys finished but timeline shows only CPU-side work. weirdly /proc/driver/nvidia is owner root:root and the container user can't read some files
alex: that matches a problem i've seen — nvidia-container-toolkit needs specific mounts for metrics and APIs. if the container runtime didn't mount /dev/nvidia* and /proc/driver/nvidia with the correct modes, nsys can't correlate GPU kernels. also need cgroup devices enabled
maria: do we want to try running the pod privileged to confirm? quick repro: privileged + mount /tmp trace to host and run nsys outside the sandbox -> full kernels show up
sam: i can try a privileged canary. but i want a less-permissive fix. any suggestions for minimum perms?
priya: try granting CAP_SYS_ADMIN (or CAP_SYS_RAWIO?) and explicitly mounting /proc/driver/nvidia and /dev/nvidiactl:/dev/nvidiactl, /dev/nvidia-uvm:/dev/nvidia-uvm, /dev/nvidia0:/dev/nvidia0. also ensure nvidia-ctk config has "allow-root": true for toolkit hook. example kubernetes bits:
```yaml
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    add: ["SYS_ADMIN"]
volumeMounts:
  - name: nvidia-proc
    mountPath: /proc/driver/nvidia
    readOnly: true
volumes:
  - name: nvidia-proc
    hostPath:
      path: /proc/driver/nvidia
```
alex: also set fsGroup or chown the trace dir so nsys can write and the toolkit can place the plugin files. we had a case where file perms in /tmp prevented the host-side agent from consuming trace meta and it looked like missing kernels
maria: another wrinkle: when using nvidia-container-toolkit with containerd + kata shim, the kata VM hides host devices unless you use passthrough. So the trace will capture CPU-side queuing but not GPU kernels. If our infra toggled runtime to kata recently that could explain the regression
sam: OK timeline — i'll spin a short repro: create a pod with CAP_SYS_ADMIN + hostPath mounts for /dev/nvidia* + /proc/driver/nvidia, run the workload, collect nsys, and upload to /shared/traces. i'll paste the command when done
infra-bot: note — privileged pods require approval from infra for cluster A. filing request INC-4521
priya: for collection command, use this inside the container (short workload):
```bash
nsys profile --sample=none --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=/tmp/short-canary \
  --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-begin=1 --capture-range-end=2 \
  --wait=1000 -- python -m canary.run --workload short
```
Then `nsys export` to get timeline `nsys export --format=sqlite --output=/shared/traces/short-canary.sqlite /tmp/short-canary.qdrep`
sam: thanks. one more thing — our runtime does kernel selection fallback when sequence length spikes. i want to check if the regression correlates with KV cache misses triggering a different kernel path (more global memory loads). any tips to correlate kernels to kv-cache hits in the trace?
alex: tag the NVTX ranges around kv cache lookup and around kernel dispatch. instrument the runtime to emit NVTX push/pop with metadata like `nvtxRangePush("kv-lookup-hit")` vs `nvtxRangePush("kv-lookup-miss")`. then nsys will show ranges stacked with kernels so you can spot which kernels fire on misses
maria: in the exported sqlite timeline, filter by `nvtx` ranges and then aggregate kernel durations by range label. we used a quick sqlite query to sum durations per nvtx label to show misses dominated expensive kernels
sam: that's perfect. i'll try the instrumenting + permissive mount repro. i'll post the trace when i have it
priya: if you hit host-policy blockers, temporary alternative is to run `nsys` on the node host against the pod's docker container (less ideal but bypasses container perms). example:
```bash
# on host
nsys profile --target-pid $(docker inspect --format '{{.State.Pid}}' $CONTAINER) --output=/var/tmp/host-trace
```
infra-bot: reminder: auditing policy requires traces with PII scrubbed before upload to S3. follow trace-sanitize.sh
sam: noted. i'll start the canary now and report back with results + traces. thanks all :thumbsup:
